claim: The adaptive radiation of pupfishes on San Salvador Island consists of three species: a generalist (Cyprinodon variegatus), a molluscivore (Cyprinodon brontotheroides), and a scale-eater (Cyprinodon desquamator).
source: This radiation is comprised of two trophic specialists, a molluscivore (durophage: Cyprinodon brontotheroides) and a scale-eater (lepidophage: Cyprinodon desquamator), derived from a Caribbean-wide generalist (Cyprinodon variegatus) which also coexists in the same habitats.
evidence: The text directly states the three species and their trophic roles.

claim: All three pupfish species occur in sympatry in the hypersaline lakes of San Salvador Island, Bahamas.
source: These three species all occur in sympatry in the hypersaline lakes of San Salvador Island, Bahamas (Figure 1a).
evidence: The text explicitly states sympatric occurrence and references Figure 1a showing the species.

claim: The three pupfish species all forage within the same benthic microhabitat with no habitat segregation observed in 14 years of field studies.
source: Found in the benthic littoral zone of each lake, all three species forage within the same benthic microhabitat; indeed, no habitat segregation has been observed in 14 years of field studies.
evidence: The text explicitly states the lack of habitat segregation based on long-term field observations.

claim: The adaptive radiation of San Salvador Island pupfishes originated less than 10,000 years ago.
source: Originating less than 10,000 years ago (based on geological age estimates for the lakes: Turner et al., 2008), the functional and trophic novelty harbored within this radiation is the product of exceptional rates of craniofacial morphological evolution (Martin and Wainwright, 2011; St John et al., 2020a; Martin et al., 2019; St John et al., 2020b).
evidence: The text cites geological age estimates from Turner et al., 2008 to support the timeframe.

claim: The pupfish radiation exhibits exceptional rates of craniofacial morphological evolution.
source: Originating less than 10,000 years ago (based on geological age estimates for the lakes: Turner et al., 2008), the functional and trophic novelty harbored within this radiation is the product of exceptional rates of craniofacial morphological evolution (Martin and Wainwright, 2011; St John et al., 2020a; Martin et al., 2019; St John et al., 2020b).
evidence: The text cites multiple studies documenting exceptional rates of morphological evolution.

source: The adaptive radiation of San Salvador Island pupfishes, like many others (Pease et al., 2016; Richards et al., 2018; Meier et al., 2017; McGee et al., 2020; Irisarri et al., 2018), appears to have originated from a complex interplay of abundant standing genetic variation, adaptive introgression from neighboring islands, and several de novo single-nucleotide mutations and deletions found only in the scale-eater (Richards et al., 2021; Richards et al., 2017).
